items.title: Hypothesis-awkward
items.text:
Hypothesis strategies for Awkward Array.

Hypothesis-awkward is a collection of Hypothesis strategies that generate Awkward Array data for tests, both of Awkward Array itself and of code that uses it. Tests written with these strategies run in Awkward Array's continuous integration (CI). Together with the package's own tests, they have found bugs in Awkward Array, PyArrow, and Hypothesis; the bugs-found log lists them. To cite Hypothesis-awkward, see Citation.

Awkward Array represents nested lists, lists of variable length, records, missing values, and values of mixed types, nested to any depth. Two arrays can hold the same values and have the same type, such as var * ?float64, yet be stored differently. Each array is stored as a layout, a tree of nodes that hold the data: the variable-length lists in this example can be stored in either of two node classes, the missing values in any of four, a list can skip data at the start of its content, the layout can contain data that no element reaches, and the buffers can be virtual, loaded only when an operation needs them. Ordinary operations, such as slicing and masking, produce many of these layouts, and the choices multiply with each level of nesting. Code that accepts Awkward Arrays is expected to work on all of them.

Many tests check predefined samples: inputs chosen by a developer, or generated by AI, and written into the test. For Awkward Array data, these samples cover a small part of the possible arrays, and the tests miss the edge cases outside it. Predefined samples also let an implementation be fitted to them: an AI coding agent, for example, can produce code that returns the expected outputs for those inputs without implementing the behavior for others. Either way, the tests pass while the code is wrong. That matters because software is developed iteratively, in cycles of refactoring and feature changes, each made safe by tests that pass only when the code behaves as expected — and AI coding agents now make the cycles shorter.

Hypothesis addresses both problems with property-based testing. A test states properties that must hold for every valid input — for example, that writing an array to a file and reading it back returns an equal array. A Hypothesis strategy describes the inputs, and Hypothesis generates many different samples from it at run time, so no sample is written into the test for an implementation to be fitted to. When a test fails, Hypothesis shrinks the failing sample to the simplest one it can find that still fails in the same way.

The main strategy of Hypothesis-awkward, st_ak.constructors.arrays() (where st_ak is hypothesis_awkward.strategies), can produce almost any layout, nested to any depth. It is layout-based: its options, listed in the API reference, allow or exclude kinds of layout nodes and limit sizes, so a test can restrict it to the arrays the code under test accepts. Generating and Shrinking Samples explains how it builds and shrinks samples. Strategies that generate arrays of a given type are planned; the Roadmap describes them.

items.title: Generating and Shrinking Samples
items.text:
When a property-based test fails, the array it reports is usually small and simple — a short list, a single small number — rather than a large, complex one. That is by design. The Testing Awkward Array page calls the reported array a "minimal failing array"; this page explains where it comes from: how hypothesis-awkward builds a random Awkward Array, and how it reduces a failing one.

Property-based testing runs one test against many generated inputs; when one input fails, Hypothesis reduces it to a simpler input that still fails — it shrinks the example. This is a detailed explanation of how the strategies work, written for Awkward Array contributors and for authors of Hypothesis strategies. If you only want to generate test arrays for your own code, start with Getting Started.

items.title: Generating a sample
items.text:
The main strategy, st_ak.constructors.arrays() (with import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak), generates a nearly fully general Awkward Array. Underneath, st_ak.constructors.contents() builds the array's layout from the top down: at each step it either stops at a leaf or chooses a wrapper layout and then builds that wrapper's child (or children) with the same strategy.

  • Leaves carry the data: an EmptyArray (no data, type unknown), a NumpyArray of one dtype, or a string or bytestring. (A string or bytestring is itself a ListOffsetArray wrapping a NumpyArray of uint8, which the strategy treats as a single leaf.)
  • Wrappers add structure around a child: RegularArray, ListOffsetArray, ListArray, RecordArray, UnionArray, IndexedArray, and the option (missing-value) types. Categorical data is also a wrapper, an IndexedArray or IndexedOptionArray, but its child is always a leaf.

Because a wrapper's child is generated by the same strategy, the layout grows recursively into a tree. Generation is bounded so that it always terminates: max_size is a budget over most of the scalar values in the layout (data elements, offsets, indices, field names, and parameters), and max_depth, max_leaf_size, min_length, and max_length constrain it further. When a layout has more than one child, the element budget is shared across them so that the total stays within max_size.

These bounds are also options a caller can set: passing a dtypes strategy, setting the allow_* flags, or fixing min_length and max_length constrains the shape of what is generated. See the API reference for every option. For example, a test can bound the depth of every generated array:

from hypothesis import given

import awkward as ak
import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak


@given(a=st_ak.constructors.arrays(max_depth=2))
def test_some_property(a: ak.Array) -> None: ...

The dtype of a NumpyArray leaf is itself drawn from a strategy, st_ak.numpy.supported_dtypes().

items.title: How Hypothesis shrinks
items.text:
When a test fails, Hypothesis searches for a simpler input that still fails. The Hypothesis guide Strategies that shrink describes the model: the engine "sees every example as a labelled tree of choices," and it "shrinks from the 'bottom up'. If any component of your strategy is replaced with a simpler example, the end result should also become simpler."

There is therefore no single setting that makes shrinking good. The quality emerges from how each choice in a strategy is arranged: if every individual choice shrinks toward something simple, the array built from those choices tends to become simpler too.

items.title: Shrinking toward simpler data
items.text:
hypothesis-awkward cannot change how Hypothesis shrinks; it can only change the order in which it offers each choice. Hypothesis's one_of() and sampled_from() both shrink toward their earlier entries — observed behavior of the shrinking engine, not a documented guarantee — so each strategy lists its alternatives simplest first. This tree of choices is the same tree the strategy built while generating, so a sample tends to shrink well when each of its choices does. The tendency is not a guarantee: when choices are coupled — one choice's simplest value depends on another that is shrinking at the same time — the composed strategy may not reach the simplest layout (see Limitations).

"Simpler" here means simpler data — what the array's values and shape look like — rather than the internal layout used to store them. For example, a list layout can hold unreachable data: content elements that no sublist refers to, left by offsets that do not start at 0 or do not reach the end of the content. Two layouts can describe the same list-of-lists while one carries unreachable data and the other does not. The strategies treat the layout without unreachable data as simpler and shrink toward it.

A contents() node also shrinks toward a leaf rather than a wrapper, and among wrappers toward RegularArray (the first wrapper offered). The scalar values inside a NumpyArray leaf are drawn by Hypothesis's own NumPy strategies, which shrink them toward zero.

items.title: What each strategy shrinks toward
items.text:
Each strategy below is in st_ak.constructors, except supported_dtypes(), which is in st_ak.numpy, and masked_contents(), which is internal.

Strategy Shrinks toward leaf_contents() EmptyArray, then bytestring, string, and NumpyArray supported_dtypes() bool, then the rest of the dtypes with a corresponding Python scalar type (int64, float64, complex128, datetime64[us], timedelta64[us]), then the remaining dtypes masked_contents() UnmaskedArray, then ByteMaskedArray, then BitMaskedArray regular_array_contents() fewer groups (a shorter outer length) with a larger size, using divisors of the content length so that no data is unreachable list_offset_array_contents() † no unreachable data: offsets[0] == 0 and offsets[-1] == len(content) list_array_contents() † no unreachable data, with contiguous, monotonic, non-overlapping starts/stops

† Best-effort and not reliably reached; see Limitations.

items.title: Verifying shrink quality
items.text:
Each shrink direction in the table has a test; the simplest is the dtype case. The tests call hypothesis.find() with the example database disabled, then assert the minimal value:

>>> from hypothesis import find, settings
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak
>>> find(st_ak.numpy.supported_dtypes(), lambda d: True, settings=settings(database=None))
dtype('bool')

find() searches for the simplest value it can find that satisfies the predicate — best-effort, like all shrinking. Here the predicate lambda d: True accepts every dtype, so the result is the simplest dtype, bool. Setting database=None stops Hypothesis from replaying a previously stored example, so the result comes only from this run and the doctest stays reproducible. The full set of shrink tests is under tests/strategies/; the tests for the two †-marked rows are the xfail cases described under Limitations.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
Shrinking is best-effort: it searches for a minimal failing example but does not guarantee the globally simplest one. The reachability of list layouts shows the limit precisely. Generating the offsets of a ListOffsetArray in isolation reliably shrinks to no unreachable data. In the composed list_offset_array_contents() and list_array_contents() strategies, however — where the child content is generated and shrunk at the same time — the shrinker does not reliably reach that layout, so those two tests are marked xfail (pytest's expected-failure marker) with the reason "shrinker does not reliably reach no-unreachable layout."

For the general theory, and advice on writing strategies that shrink well, see the Hypothesis guide Strategies that shrink.

items.title: Getting Started
items.text: By the end of this page you will have drawn generated Awkward Arrays, learned to read their reprs, run your first property-based test, and shaped what is generated. The page assumes the package is installed.

items.title: Draw your first arrays
items.text:
The main strategy, arrays(), generates Awkward Arrays — a strategy is the object Hypothesis draws test data from. To see what it produces, save this script as explore_arrays.py and run it:

import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

strategy = st_ak.constructors.arrays()
for _ in range(5):
    print(repr(strategy.example()))

python explore_arrays.py

The script prints five generated arrays. The example() method draws one sample from a strategy; it is meant for exploring a strategy interactively, not for use inside tests.

The generated arrays cover numbers (including nan and infinities), dates and durations, strings, bytestrings, records, unions, missing values, and nested lists of regular and variable length, in a variety of Awkward layouts. The API reference lists exactly which layouts are generated.

items.title: Reading the output
items.text:
• None is a missing value. NaT ("not a time") is the missing-value placeholder inside date and duration types.
  • A ? prefix or option[...] in the type string marks an option type — a type whose values can be missing. The two spellings mean the same; ? is the short form.
  • ?? marks a virtual value: the array is backed by lazy buffers that have not been computed yet, so the repr shows placeholders instead of values. This appears in the values, unlike the type-level ?.
  • Parentheses mark a record without field names, as in 2 * (string).
  • A type string reads left to right: 4 * int32 is four int32 values, and 24 * var * ?float64 is 24 variable-length lists of float64 values that can be missing. union[...] is a mixed type, and unknown is the type of an array with no actual values (an empty array, or one whose values are all missing).

items.title: Write your first property test
items.text:
The strategies are for use with Hypothesis in tests. Save this as test_arrays.py:

from hypothesis import given

import awkward as ak
import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak


@given(array=st_ak.constructors.arrays())
def test_arrays(array: ak.Array) -> None:
    assert isinstance(array, ak.Array)

The test runs with pytest, which is not installed with the package; run pip install pytest first if you do not have it. pytest collects functions whose names start with test_ in files named test_*.py. Run the test:

pytest test_arrays.py

The test passes (pytest reports 1 passed). The @given decorator ran the test function many times, each time with a newly generated array, and the assertion held for every one of them. That is a property-based test: instead of picking input arrays by hand, you state a property and Hypothesis generates the inputs — the introduction explains the idea. Here the property is only that every generated value is an ak.Array; a real test asserts a property of your own code. When an assertion fails, Hypothesis reports a minimal failing example; Generating and Shrinking Samples explains how.

items.title: Shape what is generated
items.text:
Options of arrays() narrow the output. For example, allow_virtual=False turns off virtual arrays, so no ?? placeholders appear. Change the strategy in explore_arrays.py and run it again:

import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

strategy = st_ak.constructors.arrays(allow_virtual=False)
for _ in range(5):
    print(repr(strategy.example()))

python explore_arrays.py

A run might print, for example:

<Array [] type='0 * unknown'>
<Array [[[b''], [b''], ..., [b''], [b'']], ...] type='3 * 13 * 1 * bytes'>
<Array [] type='0 * var * 1 * int32'>
<Array [b'#h\x950#\x8cMv', b'', ..., b'\xbf\xcc\x1c\xfe\xe0'] type='9 * bytes'>
<Array ['í衣䕉', ..., 'D'] type='4 * string'>

The API reference documents all options.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The package requires Python 3.11 or later.

You can install the package from PyPI using pip:

pip install hypothesis-awkward

Or from conda-forge using conda:

conda install conda-forge::hypothesis-awkward

Hypothesis and Awkward Array will be installed as dependencies if compatible versions are not already installed.

To confirm the installation, import the package:

python -c "import hypothesis_awkward"

The command prints nothing if the installation succeeded.

Once installed, see Getting Started.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text: This page describes what hypothesis-awkward generates today and where it is heading, and is reviewed at each release. It gives no dates; the order of the items reflects priority, not a schedule.

items.title: What you can generate today
items.text:
Today the main strategy, st_ak.constructors.arrays() (with import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak), generates arrays in terms of their layout — the low-level structure of an Awkward Array, a tree of Content nodes — by composing those nodes directly. It resides in the constructors subpackage because its development has followed the direct constructors section of the Awkward Array documentation.

The library includes strategies for each of EmptyArray, NumpyArray, RegularArray, ListOffsetArray, ListArray, RecordArray, UnionArray, IndexedArray, IndexedOptionArray, ByteMaskedArray, BitMaskedArray, UnmaskedArray, as well as for strings, bytestrings, and categorical data. The main strategy arrays() generates nested combinations of these, and can also generate arrays backed by virtual (lazy) buffers. Some variants of these, such as other index types and parameters, are not generated yet; they are tracked in issue #238. Getting Started shows sample outputs, and the API reference lists the available options.

The current arrays() is not exported from the top-level package, so it must be called as st_ak.constructors.arrays(). The bare name st_ak.arrays(), without constructors, is reserved for the type- and form-directed strategy described below; it does not exist yet. Today you shape generation by constraints such as the allow_* flags, dtypes, length bounds (min_length, max_length), and a total-size bound (max_size), rather than by an exact type. Asking for an array of a specific type is the next direction.

The project is at version 0.x, before 1.0, so the API can still change between releases (see the release notes).

items.title: Directions we are exploring
items.text: Awkward describes an array at three levels, from the most abstract to the most concrete: its type (the datashape, such as var * float64), its form (the structure of a layout without its data buffers; one type can have many forms, but each form has exactly one type), and its layout (the concrete tree of Content nodes that holds the data buffers). Every generated array has all three. What changes across the directions below is the level you describe it in terms of: today its layout, next its type, and later its form.

items.title: Near-term
items.text:
Generate arrays from a type. Add strategies that generate Awkward types (building on an existing internal strategy for NumPy types), then strategies that generate arrays matching a given type. This is the planned home of the reserved st_ak.arrays(). It would let a test generate arrays of the specific type that the code under test expects:

# Not yet available — illustrative of the planned type-directed API.
# st_ak.arrays() does not exist yet; today, call st_ak.constructors.arrays()
# without type=.
from hypothesis import given

import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak


@given(array=st_ak.arrays(type='var * float64'))
def test_my_analysis(array):
    result = my_analysis(array)  # my_analysis: the code under test
    # A property that should hold for every generated array:
    assert len(result) == len(array)

Here @given is the Hypothesis decorator that runs the test function repeatedly, each time on one generated array. Today the same intent is expressed through constraints instead of a type: st_ak.constructors.arrays(), narrowed with the constraints described above to the inputs the code under test accepts. See the introduction for property-based testing and Getting Started for using the current arrays().

Related work: static type stubs for Awkward data types are being explored in parallel in the personal proof-of-concept repository awkward-stubs-pilot-01. It would pair naturally with type-directed generation.

items.title: Later
items.text: Generate arrays from a form. Because one type can have many forms — a list type, for example, can be laid out as a ListOffsetArray or a ListArray — a later step is to generate forms for a given type (building on an existing internal strategy for NumPy forms), and then arrays matching a given form, also under the reserved st_ak.arrays(). This helps when a test depends on the concrete layout, not only the type.

items.title: Influencing the roadmap
items.text: These priorities are open. If you build on Awkward and need a particular type, layout, or option that the library does not yet generate, please open an issue with the use case. A concrete use case is the most useful way to shape what comes next.

items.title: Testing Awkward Array
items.text: This page is for Awkward Array contributors and for readers assessing the project. If you want to use the strategies in your own tests, start with Getting Started.

items.title: How hypothesis-awkward tests Awkward Array
items.text:
Awkward Array builds arrays by composing a small set of layout nodes (the classes in ak.contents): numeric leaves, the unknown-type EmptyArray, variable-length and regular lists, indexed (indirection) nodes, missing values in four node forms, records, and unions. The nodes compose recursively, subject to a few validity rules, so the valid arrays span a large combinatorial space of layouts. Test data written by hand covers only a small part of that space, and failures often occur on input shapes that are absent from hand-written test cases. This makes Awkward Array hard to test thoroughly.

Property-based testing inverts the approach: instead of choosing inputs, a test states a property that must hold for every valid array, and the inputs are generated. This package supplies the generation. Its main strategy is st_ak.constructors.arrays() (with import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak), which generates nearly fully general Awkward Arrays, including virtual arrays — arrays whose buffers are not yet materialized. A generated array has either all buffers virtual or none; it lives on the CPU backend and carries no node parameters other than the __array__ markers that make strings, bytestrings, and categorical data, so named record types and custom behaviors are not yet generated. See Getting Started for what it produces.

By default, arrays() can generate layouts that Awkward builds without an error but ak.is_valid() considers invalid: a UnionArray with mergeable contents and categorical data with duplicate categories. A failing example can shrink to such a layout. Pass allow_invalid=False to exclude such layouts. ak.is_valid() currently raises KeyError on categorical data with some dtypes, including complex (Awkward issue #4509).

Four kinds of properties are checked:

Round-trip. Converting an array to another representation and back reconstructs an equal array. The first property test covered ak.to_buffers() and ak.from_buffers() (the snippet is adapted from test_to_from_buffers.py):

from hypothesis import given

import awkward as ak
import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak


@given(a=st_ak.constructors.arrays())
def test_roundtrip(a: ak.Array) -> None:
    sent = ak.to_buffers(a)
    returned = ak.from_buffers(*sent)
    assert ak.array_equal(a, returned, equal_nan=True)

The same property now also covers the conversions to and from NumPy, Arrow, Parquet, Feather, and JSON. Only the buffers round trip draws from the unrestricted strategy; the other five narrow it — with the strategy's allow_* flags, restricted dtype strategies, and format-compatibility filters — to what the target format can represent, so each conversion is checked over the subset it is expected to support. Where a bug is still open, a restriction can also stand in for a known-issue predicate, with the issue cited in the test module. The NumPy round trip, for example, draws no variable-length lists, records, unions, strings, or bytestrings — regular (fixed-size) lists stay, since they become NumPy dimensions — and a separate test carries option types through NumPy masked arrays. Where a conversion cannot preserve everything, the property becomes a fixed point instead: converting the reconstructed array a second time reproduces the same result.

Equality. ak.array_equal() is reflexive (an array equals itself) and symmetric (the argument order does not change the result), with tests adapted from test_array_equal.py (the imports are the same as above):

@given(a=st_ak.constructors.arrays())
def test_reflexivity(a: ak.Array) -> None:
    assert ak.array_equal(a, a, equal_nan=True)


@given(a1=st_ak.constructors.arrays(), a2=st_ak.constructors.arrays())
def test_symmetry(a1: ak.Array, a2: ak.Array) -> None:
    forward = ak.array_equal(a1, a2, equal_nan=True)
    backward = ak.array_equal(a2, a1, equal_nan=True)
    assert forward == backward

equal_nan=True treats two NaN values as equal — and likewise two NaT (not-a-time) values in datetimes and timedeltas — which the properties need because the generated arrays can contain both.

No-raise. When the operation is expected to accept a generated array — the test judges this from the array's form and the call's arguments — it must complete without raising an error. ak.flatten(), ak.all(), ak.any(), and ak.ravel() are tested this way.

Kernel. Awkward Array specifies each low-level kernel with a pure-Python reference definition in kernel-specification.yml. Two kernels are covered so far, awkward_BitMaskedArray_to_ByteMaskedArray and awkward_BitMaskedArray_to_IndexedOptionArray: each test runs the compiled CPU kernel — and the CUDA kernel when a GPU is present — and compares the results with the reference definition. A kernel works below the layout level, so these tests draw the kernel's own arguments — a bit mask and its flags — with plain Hypothesis strategies rather than with this package's.

The round-trip, equality, and no-raise properties need no reference implementation to compare against; the kernel property is the exception, and its oracle is the specification's reference definition. When a property fails, Hypothesis shrinks the input toward a minimal failing array — a best-effort search that Generating and Shrinking Samples explains — which is why the bug reports below are small enough to reproduce by hand.

items.title: How the tests run in Awkward Array's CI
items.text:
The strategies are integrated into Awkward Array's continuous integration (CI). The first property-based tests were added in #3887 and live in tests/properties. On every change they run under the default profile in tests/properties/conftest.py, which inherits the built-in ci profile that Hypothesis loads automatically in CI: generation is derandomized — seeded from a hash of each test function — so a run repeats the same examples until the test function, the strategies, or the Hypothesis or Python version changes. A nightly run (property-tests.yml) selects the nightly profile from the same file, which raises max_examples — the number of valid examples each test tries — and turns randomization back on, so it reaches examples the per-change runs never generate. The nightly run also reports Hypothesis's run statistics — how many examples each test generated and how many were invalid — which keeps the discard rate visible as the predicates below accumulate. A second nightly workflow (property-tests-gpu.yml) runs the kernel test on a GPU under the same nightly profile.

Awkward Array pins hypothesis-awkward to an exact version, and Dependabot proposes an update for each release: a new strategy release changes which inputs are generated, and the pin keeps that change from surfacing as an unrelated failure in someone else's pull request. Upstream test pull requests lists the pull requests that built this arrangement.

A bug that stays open does not block the suite. Where the tests would otherwise reach it, its trigger is encoded as a predicate on the array, named after its issue number (has_issue_4262, for example) — shared predicates live in known_issues.py, and a module that is alone affected keeps private ones next to its tests — and the affected draws are discarded, with Hypothesis's assume() inside the test or by filtering the strategy. A predicate is deleted in the pull request that fixes its issue, so the discarded inputs are tested again. The predicates are reviewed and merged in Awkward Array itself (#4275, #4281), so the open bugs these tests reach are acknowledged in the library's own test suite. The suite keeps passing while every open bug remains visible in the issue tracker and in the log below.

items.title: What the bugs show
items.text:
The bugs found so far (listed in Bugs found below) are not spread evenly over Awkward Array; they cluster where generated inputs have an advantage over hand-written ones.

Conversion boundaries. The largest group of the bugs is in the conversions — ak.to_numpy(), ak.to_arrow(), ak.from_json(), ak.from_parquet(), and their inverses. A conversion must map every valid layout onto another system's representation, so each rarely-exercised layout feature is a chance for a mismatch. Round-trip properties probe exactly that mapping, in both directions.

Rare but valid shapes. The triggers are almost never the common cases; they are empty unions, zero-length lists, missing values in unusual places, offsets that do not start at zero, and uncommon dtypes such as datetime64[D] or float16. A developer writing test data by hand rarely constructs these; a generator that samples the whole layout space constructs them routinely.

Beyond the library under test. The tests also exercise the software around Awkward Array. The Feather round trip — ak.to_feather() writes Arrow's inter-process communication (IPC) file format — produced invalid files whose cause is in PyArrow's IPC writer; it was reported upstream after reducing to a pure-PyArrow case. And one bug was in Hypothesis itself: after shrinking a failing array, its explain phase ended in an internal assertion error.

items.title: Bugs found
items.text: Tests written with these strategies — in Awkward Array's suite and in hypothesis-awkward's own — have found bugs in Awkward Array, in PyArrow, and in Hypothesis. This log is reviewed at each release; status is as of the last review. The Awkward Array list is grouped by the operation involved, ascending by number within each group; "fixed" points to the merged fixing pull request, and an entry says so where the fix is not yet in a released Awkward version.

items.title: Awkward Array
items.text:
Equality:

  • #3888 (fixed in #3909) — ak.array_equal() raised an error on virtual arrays and returned the wrong result for empty unions.
  • #3921 (reported and fixed in this pull request) — ak.array_equal() returned the wrong result for datetimes and timedeltas containing NaT.
  • #3962 (reported and fixed in this pull request) — ak.almost_equal(), which backs ak.array_equal(), compared record-array fields incorrectly.
  • #4316 (open) — ak.array_equal() returns False for equal unions whose list-of-records child is indexed in a different order.

NumPy conversion:

  • #4217 (open) — ak.to_numpy() fails for option-type timedelta64 arrays that contain missing values.
  • #4226 (open) — ak.from_numpy() fails for multidimensional masked string arrays with no masked elements.
  • #4227 (fixed in #4423) — ak.from_numpy() raised a ValueError for masked arrays of three or more dimensions with a zero-length dimension; the fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.

Arrow conversion:

  • #4219 (closed, no linked fix) — ak.to_arrow() silently corrupted datetime64[D] values.
  • #4221 (open) — ak.to_arrow() raises an IndexError for a non-empty option array with zero-length list content.
  • #4222 (fixed in #4407) — ak.to_arrow() silently shifted list values when a nullable list's offsets did not start at zero; the fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.
  • #4228 (open) — ak.to_arrow() raises an IndexError for valid unions with option-type children.
  • #4229 (open) — ak.from_arrow() loses the length of a size-0 fixed-size list.
  • #4230 (open) — ak.from_arrow() raises an AttributeError for a table with a null-type column.
  • #4255 (open) — ak.from_arrow() fails on an option record with an IndexedArray-of-EmptyArray field.
  • #4274 (open) — ak.to_arrow_table() fails for an UnmaskedArray of records with a uint32-indexed field.

Parquet conversion:

  • #4220 (open) — ak.from_parquet() fails on NaT or out-of-range datetime64[ms]/[us] row-group statistics.
  • #4305 (fixed in #4396) — the ak.to_parquet()/ak.from_parquet() round trip raised an AssertionError on an UnmaskedArray field of a record with null rows; the fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.

Feather conversion:

  • #4238 (fixed in #4441) — ak.to_feather() wrote union-type arrays as invalid files, and ak.from_feather() crashed reading them; the cause was #50623 in PyArrow's IPC writer. The fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.

JSON conversion:

  • #4241 (open) — ak.from_json() parses floats at reduced precision, so values drift on each reparse.
  • #4242 (fixed in #4391) — ak.from_json() raised a TypeError when JSON mixed null with heterogeneous values; the fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.
  • #4243 (open) — ak.from_json() silently wraps JSON integers in [2**63, 2**64) to negative int64 values.
  • #4244 (open) — ak.to_json() writes lone-surrogate escapes that ak.from_json() rejects.

Flattening and broadcasting:

  • #4214 (fixed in #4246) — ak.flatten(axis=None) dropped data or raised an IndexError on nested unions, a regression in Awkward Array 2.11.0.
  • #4247 (open) — ak.broadcast_arrays() silently skips broadcasting on some union-containing arrays.
  • #4260 (open) — ak.flatten() with a negative axis raises an AssertionError when record field depths differ.
  • #4261 (open) — ak.ravel() raises internal errors when the collected leaves cannot merge.
  • #4262 (open) — ak.broadcast_arrays() fails for a flat array and a regular list of variable-length lists.
  • #4263 (fixed in #4292) — ak.ravel() raised an AssertionError with no message on a union that no values reach.
  • #4278 (open) — ak.ravel() raises an OverflowError when temporal leaves need an overflowing unit conversion.
  • #4280 (open) — ak.ravel() raises an OverflowError when a temporal value does not fit the merged unit.
  • #4282 (fixed in #4303) — ak.ravel() failed or silently reordered values when a union branch was an all-regular list.
  • #4283 (open) — ak.ravel() raises an AssertionError on a record under an option beside a non-record leaf.
  • #4291 (fixed in #4292) — ak.ravel() raised an AssertionError when zero-field records left nothing to merge.
  • #4297 (fixed in #4303) — ak.ravel() failed or silently dropped values when a union branch was a single-field record.

Reducers and sorting:

  • #4259 (fixed in #4270) — nearly all reducers and sorting raised a KeyError on float16, float128, and complex256 leaves; the fix is not yet in a released version as of the last review.
  • #4264 (open) — reducers fail on an option type inside a RegularArray's untrimmed content.

Layout internals and virtual arrays:

  • #4126 (fixed in #4127) — ak.contents.IndexedOptionArray.to_ByteMaskedArray raised an unhelpful TypeError when a non-empty array's content was an EmptyArray; the fix rejects the conversion with a clear error.
  • #4288 (fixed in #4293) — virtual arrays lost the length of a nested zero-field RecordArray.

A NumPy property test in test_numpy_arrays.py accounts for #3690 (open): ak.to_numpy() does not support structured arrays whose fields are not one-dimensional. This is a pre-existing limitation the tests work around, not a bug they found.

items.title: PyArrow
items.text: • #50623 (fixed) — Arrow's IPC serialization dropped a union's buffers when the union was wrapped in an extension type, producing invalid data that segfaulted on read. Reported with a pure-PyArrow reproduction after the Feather round trip surfaced it as #4238. Fixed in #50927 and released in PyArrow 26.0.0.

items.title: Hypothesis
items.text: • #4708 (fixed) — an AssertionError in Shrinker.explain() for unstable span labels. Fixed in #4717 and released in Hypothesis 6.152.4.

items.title: Outlook
items.text: The goal is to cover all testable properties of Awkward Array — more operations, slicing, reducers, and the remaining kernels — following the pattern the suite has established: add a property test, file the bugs it finds, and discard their triggers until the fixes are merged. Automatically generated test inputs raise confidence that a change is correct across a broad range of valid arrays, not only the cases a developer wrote by hand.

items.text:
Strategies that build Awkward Arrays and their layouts with direct constructors.

These strategies follow the Awkward Array User Guide section "Direct constructors": they build layouts, i.e., trees of Content nodes, by calling the constructors of the Content subclasses directly.

arrays() wraps a layout in an ak.Array; the other strategies generate layouts. contents() generates the layouts that arrays() wraps. Each *_array_contents() strategy generates one Content subclass; leaf_contents() chooses among the leaf classes, and option_contents() among the option-type classes; and string_contents(), bytestring_contents(), and categorical_contents() generate the layouts of strings, bytestrings, and categorical data.

The strategies are listed in the order of the guide section.

    allow_virtual: bool = True,
) -> SearchStrategy[Array]

Strategy for Awkward Arrays.

This is the main strategy of hypothesis-awkward. The aim is to generate fully general Awkward Arrays, with many options to control layout, data types, missing values, masks, and other array attributes.

In constructing arrays, this strategy follows the Awkward Array User Guide section "Direct constructors". It constructs layouts and wraps them in an ak.Array. The layouts are instances of subclasses of Content.

By default, when called with no arguments, arrays() generates the most general arrays currently implemented, subject to a finite maximum size. Arguments can be provided to exclude certain layouts or data types, or to constrain values and sizes.

The current implementation generates arrays with the following layouts:

  • EmptyArray
  • NumpyArray
  • RegularArray
  • ListArray
  • ListOffsetArray
  • Strings
  • Bytestrings
  • RecordArray
  • IndexedArray
  • Categorical data
  • IndexedOptionArray
  • ByteMaskedArray
  • BitMaskedArray
  • UnmaskedArray
  • UnionArray

Each type can be excluded separately with the corresponding allow_* argument.

max_size is the main argument for constraining the array size. It counts most of the scalar values in the layout, including data elements, offsets, indices, field names, and parameters. The array size can also be constrained with max_leaf_size, max_depth, min_length, and max_length.

arrays() randomly generates virtual arrays by lazifying buffers. allow_virtual=False disables virtual arrays.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dtypes SearchStrategy[dtype] | None

A strategy for NumPy scalar dtypes used in NumpyArray. If None, the default strategy that generates any scalar dtype supported by Awkward Array is used. Does not affect string or bytestring content.

None max_size int

Upper bound on the number of scalars in the generated content. Counts data elements, offsets, indices, field names, and parameters.

50 allow_nan bool

No NaN/NaT values are generated in NumpyArray if False.

True allow_invalid bool

Layouts that ak.validity_error and ak.is_valid consider invalid can be generated if True: UnionArray with mergeable contents and categorical data with duplicate categories. Examples can shrink to such layouts. Every generated layout is valid if False.

True allow_numpy bool

No NumpyArray is generated if False.

True allow_empty bool

No EmptyArray is generated if False. EmptyArray has Awkward type unknown and carries no data. Unlike NumpyArray, it is unaffected by dtypes and allow_nan.

True allow_string bool

No string content is generated if False. A string is represented as a ListOffsetArray wrapping a NumpyArray(uint8). Each character (uint8) and offset in the ListOffsetArray counts toward max_size. A string is considered a single leaf element in counting toward max_leaf_size and max_depth. Each string (not character) counts toward max_leaf_size. A string does not count toward max_depth. Unaffected by dtypes and allow_nan.

True allow_bytestring bool

No bytestring content is generated if False. A bytestring is represented as a ListOffsetArray wrapping a NumpyArray(uint8). Each byte (uint8) and offset in the ListOffsetArray counts toward max_size. A bytestring is considered a single leaf element in counting toward max_leaf_size and max_depth. Each bytestring (not byte) counts toward max_leaf_size. A bytestring does not count toward max_depth. Unaffected by dtypes and allow_nan.

True allow_regular bool

No RegularArray is generated if False.

True allow_list_offset bool

No ListOffsetArray is generated if False.

True allow_list bool

No ListArray is generated if False.

True allow_record bool

No RecordArray is generated if False. This includes records with no fields.

True allow_union bool

No UnionArray is generated if False.

True allow_indexed bool

No IndexedArray is generated if False.

True allow_indexed_option bool

No IndexedOptionArray is generated if False.

True allow_categorical bool

No categorical data is generated if False. Categorical data is an IndexedArray or an IndexedOptionArray, so allow_indexed and allow_indexed_option also apply to it.

True allow_byte_masked bool

No ByteMaskedArray is generated if False.

True allow_bit_masked bool

No BitMaskedArray is generated if False.

True allow_unmasked bool

No UnmaskedArray is generated if False.

True max_leaf_size int | None

Maximum total number of leaf elements in the generated content. Each numerical value, including complex and datetime, counts as one. Each string and bytestring (not character or byte) counts as one.

None max_depth int | None

Maximum nesting depth. Each RegularArray, ListOffsetArray, ListArray, RecordArray, and UnionArray layer adds one level, excluding those that form string or bytestring content. No constraint when None (the default).

None min_length int

Minimum len() of the generated array.

0 max_length int | None

Maximum len() of the generated array. No constraint when None (the default).

None min_record_fields int

Minimum number of fields in each generated RecordArray, at any nesting depth. If 1 or greater, no records with no fields are generated. No RecordArray is generated when it exceeds max_record_fields.

0 max_record_fields int | None

Maximum number of fields in each generated RecordArray, at any nesting depth. Unbounded if None. If 0, only records with no fields are generated.

None allow_virtual bool

No virtual arrays are generated if False.

True

Examples:

>>> import awkward as ak
>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

Test code that takes an Awkward Array. Here, ak.to_list() stands for the code under test:

>>> @given(a=st_ak.constructors.arrays())
... def test_to_list(a):
...     assert len(ak.to_list(a)) == len(a)
>>> test_to_list()

Limit the length:

>>> @given(a=st_ak.constructors.arrays(min_length=1, max_length=3))
... def test_length(a):
...     assert 1 <= len(a) <= 3
>>> test_length()

    contents: list[Content]
    | SearchStrategy[list[Content]]
    | None = None,

    max_fields: int = 5,
    allow_tuple: bool = True,
    min_length: int = 0,
    max_length: int | None = None,
) -> SearchStrategy[RecordArray]

Strategy for ak.contents.RecordArray instances.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default contents list[Content] | SearchStrategy[list[Content]] | None

Child contents. Can be a strategy for a list of Content, a concrete list, or None to draw random children.

None max_fields int

Maximum number of fields when contents is None.

5 allow_tuple bool

Allow tuple records (no field names) if True.

True min_length int

Lower bound on the record length, i.e., len(result).

0 max_length int | None

Upper bound on the record length, i.e., len(result).

None Notes

With at least one field, the length is derived from the children as min(len(c) for c in contents), capped by max_length. A record with no fields has no children and stores no data, so nothing derives its length; it is drawn between min_length and max_length instead. When max_length is None, the ceiling is an internal value, raised to min_length if that is larger.

>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

...     )
... )

...     assert 2 <= len(c) <= 4

... def test_named(c):
...     assert not c.is_tuple

...     )

categorical_contents(
    content: SearchStrategy[Content]
    | Content
    | None = None,
    *,
    min_size: int = 0,
    max_size: int | None = None,
    allow_invalid: bool = True,
    allow_indexed: bool = True,
    allow_indexed_option: bool = True,
) -> SearchStrategy[IndexedArray | IndexedOptionArray]

Strategy for layouts of categorical data.

Categorical data is an IndexedArray or an IndexedOptionArray with the parameter __array__ set to 'categorical'. Its content holds the categories, and the index refers to them. The categories are a 1-D NumpyArray, an EmptyArray, string content, or bytestring content.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default content SearchStrategy[Content] | Content | None

The categories. Can be a strategy for Content, a concrete Content instance, or None to draw from leaf_contents(). They must be of a kind listed above and, if allow_invalid is False, unique. A concrete content that is not raises ValueError; draws from a strategy that are not are rejected. Empty categories can be referred to only by missing entries, so they are rejected if min_size > 0 and allow_indexed_option is False.

None min_size int

Lower bound on the index length, i.e., len(result).

0 max_size int | None

Upper bound on the index length, i.e., len(result). If None, twice the content length is used.

None allow_invalid bool

Duplicate categories can occur if True, which ak.validity_error and ak.is_valid consider invalid. No two categories are equal if False, as Awkward Array defines it: 0.0 and -0.0 are equal, NaNs are distinct, and at most one NaT occurs. A content of a kind not listed above is rejected regardless of this option.

True allow_indexed bool

No IndexedArray is generated if False.

True allow_indexed_option bool

No IndexedOptionArray is generated if False.

True

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If both allow_indexed and allow_indexed_option are False, or if a concrete content is not valid as categories.

Examples:

>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

Give the categories as a strategy, here for strings:

... def test_no_missing(c):

>>> test_no_missing()

Generate two values (start, end) from a strategy, where start <= end.

The minimum and maximum values can be specified by min_start, max_start, min_end, max_end.

start (end) can be None if allow_start_none (allow_end_none) is True.

If let_end_none_if_start_none is True, end will be always None when start is None regardless of allow_end_none.

If allow_equal is False, start and end cannot be equal, i.e., start < end.

Examples:

>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> from hypothesis import strategies as st
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

The pair can be passed to any strategy that takes a minimum and a maximum. Here, they are min_length and max_length:

>>> @given(data=st.data())
... def test_lengths(data):
...     min_length, max_length = data.draw(
...         st_ak.misc.ranges(min_start=0, max_end=5, allow_start_none=False)
...     )
...     c = data.draw(
...         st_ak.constructors.list_offset_array_contents(
...             min_length=min_length, max_length=max_length
...         )
...     )
...     assert min_length <= len(c)
...     assert max_length is None or len(c) <= max_length
>>> test_lengths()

Strategies for NumPy dtypes and arrays that Awkward Array supports.

supported_dtypes() generates scalar dtypes, numpy_dtypes() also generates structured dtypes, and numpy_arrays() generates NumPy arrays that can be converted to Awkward Arrays.

items.title: supported_dtypes
items.text:
supported_dtypes() -> SearchStrategy[dtype]

Strategy for NumPy dtypes supported by Awkward Array.

Datetime and timedelta dtypes are drawn with single units only, e.g., datetime64[m], not with multiples such as datetime64[10m], which Awkward Array also supports.

Examples:

>>> import awkward as ak
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

Every drawn dtype can be the dtype of a NumpyArray:

>>> @given(d=st_ak.numpy.supported_dtypes())
... def test_numpy_array(d):
...     assert ak.contents.NumpyArray(np.zeros(3, dtype=d)).dtype == d
>>> test_numpy_array()

items.title: numpy_dtypes
items.text:
numpy_dtypes(
    *,
    dtype: dtype | SearchStrategy[dtype] | None = None,
    allow_array: bool = True,
    max_size: int = 5,
) -> SearchStrategy[dtype]

Strategy for dtypes (simple or array) supported by Awkward Array.

Examples of simple dtypes are dtype('int32'), dtype('float64')

Array dtypes include ([('f0', 'i4'), ('f1', 'f8')]). They are dtypes of structured NumPy arrays.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dtype dtype | SearchStrategy[dtype] | None

A simple dtype or a strategy for simple dtypes for determining the type of array elements. If None, any supported simple dtype is used.

None allow_array bool

Generate only simple dtypes if False, else array dtypes as well.

True max_size int

Maximum number of scalars in a structured dtype.

5

Examples:

>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

Exclude structured dtypes:

>>> @given(d=st_ak.numpy.numpy_dtypes(allow_array=False))
... def test_simple(d):
...     assert d.names is None
>>> test_simple()

items.title: numpy_arrays
items.text:
numpy_arrays(
    *,
    dtype: dtype | SearchStrategy[dtype] | None = None,
    allow_structured: bool = True,
    allow_nan: bool = True,
    min_dims: int = 1,
    max_dims: int | None = None,
    min_size: int = 0,
    max_size: int = 10,
    unique: bool = False,
) -> SearchStrategy[ndarray]

Strategy for NumPy arrays from which Awkward Arrays can be created.

The arrays can be converted with ak.from_numpy(). The Awkward Array User Guide section "How to convert to/from NumPy" describes how structured and multidimensional arrays are converted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dtype dtype | SearchStrategy[dtype] | None

A simple dtype or a strategy for simple dtypes for determining the type of array elements. If None, any supported simple dtype is used.

None allow_structured bool

Generate only simple arrays if False, else structured arrays as well.

True allow_nan bool

Generate potentially NaN for relevant dtypes if True.

True min_dims int

Minimum number of dimensions.

1 max_dims int | None

Maximum number of dimensions. If None, auto-derived from max_size.

None min_size int

Minimum number of scalars in the array. For structured dtypes, each element counts as multiple scalars (one per field).

0 max_size int

Maximum number of scalars in the array. For structured dtypes, each element counts as multiple scalars (one per field).

10 unique bool

No two elements are equal if True. Only simple dtypes are generated (no structured dtypes). The achievable size is bounded by the number of distinct values the dtype can represent; when dtype is None or a strategy, dtypes that cannot supply min_size distinct values (for example bool when min_size > 2) are not drawn, and Hypothesis raises Unsatisfiable if the strategy draws only such dtypes. A single dtype that cannot supply them raises ValueError.

False

Examples:

>>> import awkward as ak
>>> from hypothesis import given
>>> import hypothesis_awkward.strategies as st_ak

Convert the arrays with ak.from_numpy():

>>> @given(n=st_ak.numpy.numpy_arrays())
... def test_from_numpy(n):
...     assert len(ak.from_numpy(n)) == len(n)
>>> test_from_numpy()

Limit the number of dimensions and exclude structured arrays:

>>> @given(n=st_ak.numpy.numpy_arrays(max_dims=2, allow_structured=False))
... def test_options(n):
...     assert n.ndim <= 2
...     assert n.dtype.names is None
>>> test_options()
